entries.label: Why are you interested in Duolingo?
entries.value: What draws me to Duolingo is that it's an education product with a real user on the other side and measurable failure modes. Most of what I've built lives in that same space. I shipped ClarityAtlas, an iOS health app, into a live Hopkins pilot with 30+ users, and the hardest part wasn't the passive sleep-estimation system I built on HealthKit and Core Motion signals like step count and gait speed. It was figuring out what people would actually open the app for. I learned the same lesson earlier with SnapSort, an AI photo-sorting product I built on Flask and AWS and grew to 300+ users: a technically functional system and a product people use are very different things. Duolingo runs experiments against half a billion learners, which means product questions get answered with data rather than opinion, and that's the kind of feedback loop I want to build inside. I'm also interested in teaching and evaluation as a technical problem, which is close to the core of what a learning product has to get right.
entries.reason: Essay generated from the operator's about-me context

entries.label: Share with us your proudest accomplishment. This can be pre-college.
entries.value: My independent research on Valley Fever, which I started in high school. I grew up around the environmental conditions the disease tracks with, and I wanted to know whether dust and agricultural activity could explain case patterns. I built an SIR-style epidemiological model in Python starting from the differential equations rather than a library, because I wanted to actually understand what each term was doing, and then connected the disease dynamics to environmental variables. I also programmed a microcontroller-based dust sensor in C/C++ so the environmental side wasn't purely theoretical. The work became a sole-author publication in the Journal of Student Research and I was selected as a national finalist in the Junior Science and Humanities Symposium. I'm proud of it less for the outcomes than because it was the first time I stopped treating math as a self-contained exercise and used it to explain something happening around me. Almost everything I've built since, from health models to anomaly detection, comes out of that shift.
entries.reason: Essay generated from the operator's about-me context

entries.label: How will your personal experiences make an impact at Duolingo?
entries.value: The most useful habit I'd bring is changing my mind when evidence contradicts me. Over the past year I've independently studied how scientific research gets funded and evaluated, and I started with a confident thesis: that grant-writing time was the main constraint on science and that compensation was pushing talented people out of academia. Interviews with researchers, administrators, and science-policy people broke both claims. The more interesting effect turned out to be selection, meaning researchers learn which ideas are legible enough to survive review and never attempt the ones that aren't, and many people knowingly trade compensation for autonomy. Sitting with that changed how I approach product work too. At Open Health Intelligence, my cofounders and I spotted President Ron Daniels through the locked doors of Garland Hall and knocked until we got to pitch him, which turned into a formal meeting months later with Data Science and AI Institute leadership. On a team that makes fact-based decisions and experiments constantly, I'd be comfortable proposing a strong hypothesis and equally comfortable being the person who says it didn't hold.
entries.reason: Essay generated from the operator's about-me context

entries.label: Tell us about your experience in computer science. Why did you choose computer science?
entries.value: I came to computer science through problems rather than through the field itself. I study Applied Mathematics and Statistics and Economics at Hopkins, and I kept running into questions where the math was only useful if I could build the system around it. That's how I ended up writing most of my work in code. The range has been wide on purpose. On a Gates Foundation-funded Hopkins / South African MRC health-equity project I was lead model developer, training XGBoost models on a national survey dataset of roughly 10 million records, using SHAP for feature selection, and designing G-formula causal simulations for counterfactual interventions. At Summer Atlantic Capital I own large parts of an anomaly-detection system, including the event-ingestion pipeline, a versioned FastAPI microservice, temporal sequence models over event streams, and a learning-to-rank layer for alert prioritization. I chose computer science because it's the fastest way I know to test whether an idea survives contact with a real user. Building is how I find out what I was wrong about.
entries.reason: Essay generated from the operator's about-me context

entries.label: Is there anything else not listed on your resume that you would like to share with us?
entries.value: One thing not on my resume is how much I think about where automation should stop. I built a Playwright-based job-application agent in TypeScript because job hunting is full of repetitive browser work, but I deliberately designed it as a deterministic operator-controlled system rather than an autonomous agent. Every application moves through an explicit state machine, SQLite is the single source of truth because browser automation gets dangerous when state diverges across processes, and every mutating capability sits behind fail-closed flags that never default on. Free-text essays and demographic fields are architecturally prevented from being auto-filled and always generate a human-review item. I also built a validation ladder so a capability isn't called working just because it passed against a local fixture. Workday and iCIMS are detected and skipped rather than handled unreliably, which was a deliberate choice to do less badly. That instinct came out of evaluation work at Intelehealth, where I compared LLM-generated clinical outputs against a 4,169-case standard and learned that generating an answer is cheap and deciding whether to trust it is the hard part.
